new_statements.quote: 彝语中的每个音节都有声调。但各地的声调数量多少不等,一般有 3-5 个声调。彝语南部方言双柏话有高平、中平、低降三个声调。彝语除了有声调外,有些音节还带有表意重音或表情重音。重音是相连的音节中某个音节发音突出的现象,它出现在句子中,同时也出现在某些语言的单词中。如云南双柏彝语: do2'love33 [scanned; sibling reading do21lo55ve33] "得了!"或"够了!" (看见异常情况时所发出来的自然感叹声或紧急呼声) ... 这类摹描自然声响的象声词和叹词,都带表意重音或表情重音。另外,彝语的表意重音有区别词汇意义和语法意义的作用。
new_statements.translation: Every syllable in Yi has a tone, but the number of tones differs from place to place, generally 3-5. The Shuangbai speech of the Southern dialect of Yi has three tones: high level, mid level, low falling. Besides tones, some syllables in Yi also carry meaning-bearing stress (biaoyi zhongyin) or expressive stress (biaoqing zhongyin). Stress is the phenomenon of one syllable among adjacent syllables being pronounced prominently; it occurs in sentences and also in the words of some languages. E.g. Shuangbai Yi of Yunnan: do2'love33 'that's it!' / 'enough!' (a natural exclamation or urgent cry on seeing something unusual) ... Such sound-imitating onomatopoeia and interjections all carry meaning-bearing or expressive stress. In addition, Yi meaning-bearing stress serves to distinguish lexical and grammatical meaning.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yi (the Southern dialect included) is a tone language (three tones in the illustrated variety); there is no positional word-stress rule. What the tradition calls stress is a lexically/grammatically contrastive 'meaning-bearing stress' or an 'expressive stress' on certain syllables, chiefly in interjections and onomatopoeia and in some words. The pan-Yi handbook (Chen, Bian & Li 1985, snippet) adds that this stress falls mostly on the first syllable of polysyllabic words, rarely on monosyllables or on second/third syllables; Chen 1963 (Xide Nuosu) says it falls on the first syllable of polysyllabic content words.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for this variety. Chen et al. 1985 (pan-Yi): some occurrences on monosyllables and on 2nd/3rd syllables of polysyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about Yi in general with Shuangbai (E-Xin = Northern/Northwestern Nisu, nort2718 [yiv]) and Liangshan examples, not the Yuan-Jin (Yuanjiang-Mojiang) vernacular; it covers sentence-level prominence and lexically contrastive stress on some words; snippet-only access, so the surrounding text (any Yuan-Jin datapoint, positions, examples) is unseen.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: yuan1242 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO code yym 'Yi, Yuanjiang-Mojiang', split on 2008-01-14 (CR 2007-086) into Southern Nisu [nsd] sout2723 and Southwestern Nisu [nsv] sout3128 (the latter marked spurious by Glottolog). In Chinese classification it is the Yuan-Jin 元金 (Yuanjiang-Jinping) vernacular of the Southern dialect of Yi (Chen, Bian & Li 1985) = Zhu Wenxu 2005 Yuan-Mo 元墨 / Southwestern vernacular: Nisu (autonym ne33su55pho21) of Honghe, Yuanyang, Jinping, Mojiang, Pu'er, Jiangcheng and Yuanjiang counties, Yunnan. Yang 2009 re-assigns the Mojiang, Jiangcheng and Lvchun varieties to North-Central Nisu east2349 [nos]. The only stress wording found (Li 1996 snippet) is pan-Yi and illustrated from Shuangbai, i.e. Northwestern Nisu nort2718 [yiv], not from a Yuanjiang or Mojiang datapoint.
